title: Cost and capacity estimation
story:
Every design decision has a cost that will only be discovered after it is built, and the alternatives usually differ by factors large enough that guessing wrongly is expensive. Estimation is how you find out beforehand — and the point is not accuracy. The point is to tell a hundred apart from a hundred thousand, because that is the distinction that changes the design.

The figures that make this possible are order-of-magnitude latencies. Dean's 2009 keynote carried the table: a first-level cache reference around half a nanosecond, a branch mispredict around five, a main memory reference around a hundred, sending two kilobytes over a gigabit network around twenty thousand, reading a megabyte sequentially from memory around two hundred and fifty thousand, a round trip within the same datacenter around five hundred thousand, a disk seek around ten million, and reading a megabyte sequentially from disk around thirty million.

Read those as ratios rather than as values, because the ratios are the content. Memory is a hundred times a cache reference. A datacenter round trip is five thousand times a memory reference. A disk seek is twenty times a datacenter round trip. And the conclusion frequently drawn from the table is the one most people find surprising: writes to the network within a datacenter are much faster than writes to local disk. If your instinct says the network is the slow part, that instinct was formed on a different problem.

Estimation then proceeds by arithmetic you can do aloud. Requests per second times bytes per request gives bandwidth. Items times bytes per item gives storage, and storage times replication factor gives what you actually buy. Concurrent work equals arrival rate times duration, which is the queuing relationship from earlier in this track and is the one that catches people, because duration includes the waiting.

The caution to carry is about the figures rather than the method. They age, and they age at different rates — bandwidth improves much more quickly than latency across disks, networks, memories and processors, by more than the square as a rule of thumb. So a stored estimate built on remembered constants is wrong in a way that is invisible until somebody checks the constants. The ratios drift more slowly than the absolute values, which is the practical reason to memorise relationships rather than numbers.

problem.name: Order-of-magnitude estimation
problem.shape: A design must be chosen before it exists, and the choice turns on quantities nobody has measured.
tell: two designs are being compared on intuition about what is fast
nobody can say how much storage the proposal needs
a capacity number was produced without stating its assumptions
the estimate uses remembered constants and nobody knows their age
problem.move: Work to one significant figure using remembered ratios, and write the assumptions beside the answer so the estimate can be rechecked rather than believed. Estimate bandwidth as rate times size, storage as count times size times replication, and concurrency as arrival rate times duration including waiting.
problem.invariant: The purpose is to separate orders of magnitude rather than to be accurate, because the decision the estimate informs almost never turns on the second significant figure.
problem.breaks: The constants age at different rates, with bandwidth improving far faster than latency, so an estimate that was right when written can become wrong without anything about the design changing. Ratios drift more slowly than absolute values, which is why memorising relationships survives where memorising numbers does not.

cost.time: minutes, against a build that may take months in the wrong direction
cost.beats: benchmarking, which is more accurate and requires the thing to exist, and intuition, which is free and systematically wrong about the network being slower than disk

worked.problem: What is a back-of-the-envelope estimate actually for?
worked.reasoning:
Separating orders of magnitude, so a design decision can be made before the thing exists. It is not a prediction and it is not a budget.

The reason it works is that the decisions worth making rarely turn on a factor of two. They turn on whether something is thousands or billions — whether this fits in memory or needs a disk, whether one machine suffices or a hundred do, whether a design is possible at all. A calculation to one significant figure answers those, and a calculation to three answers them no better while costing much more and inviting false confidence.

The inputs are a handful of remembered order-of-magnitude figures. From the 2009 table: a main memory reference around a hundred nanoseconds, a datacenter round trip around five hundred thousand, a disk seek around ten million, a megabyte read sequentially from disk around thirty million. Held as ratios, that says memory is roughly a hundred times a cache reference, a datacenter round trip is roughly five thousand memory references, and a disk seek is roughly twenty datacenter round trips.

The conclusion I would make sure to state, because it inverts most people's instinct: writes to the network within a datacenter are much faster than writes to local disk. Anyone estimating from a feeling that the network is the slow component will get the answer backwards, and that feeling is common because it is true across the internet and false within a building.

The arithmetic is then deliberately simple. Bandwidth is rate times size per item. Storage is count times size, multiplied by the replication factor, because what you buy is not what you store. Concurrency is arrival rate times duration — the queuing relationship — and the trap there is that duration means time in the system including waiting, not service time, which is why a system can need far more concurrent capacity than the service time suggests.

And the caution, which is about the constants rather than the method. They age at different rates: bandwidth improves much faster than latency, by more than the square as a rule of thumb. So an estimate built on memorised values can be wrong without the design changing, and it will be wrong invisibly. The ratios drift more slowly than the absolutes, which is the practical argument for remembering relationships and re-deriving numbers rather than the reverse.

The last part is the discipline that makes an estimate useful to anyone else: write the assumptions next to the answer. An estimate whose inputs are recorded can be rechecked when reality disagrees. An estimate that arrives as a single number gets believed or dismissed, and neither is useful.

problem.practice: Estimate the storage your largest table will need in a year: rows per day, bytes per row, days, replication factor. Write the four assumptions down. Then look up the actual current size and see which assumption was wrong — it will be one of them, and knowing which is the point.

beats.fix: Estimate before building, using order-of-magnitude figures and arithmetic rather than precision — the purpose is to tell a hundred apart from a hundred thousand, not to be accurate.
beats.cost: The figures age at different rates and some age fast, so an estimate built on memorised constants is wrong in a way that is invisible until the constants are checked.

interview.q: What is a back-of-the-envelope estimate actually for?
interview.trap: Treating it as a prediction to be made accurate. It exists to separate orders of magnitude, and the most valuable thing it does is overturn instinct — most people estimate as though the network were slower than local disk, which is false inside a datacenter.
interview.answer:
Separating orders of magnitude, so a design decision can be made before the thing exists. It is not a prediction and not a budget.

It works because decisions worth making rarely turn on a factor of two. They turn on whether something is thousands or billions — fits in memory or needs a disk, one machine or a hundred, possible at all. The inputs are remembered order-of-magnitude figures: a main memory reference around a hundred nanoseconds, a datacenter round trip around five hundred thousand, a disk seek around ten million, a megabyte read sequentially from disk around thirty million. As ratios: memory is roughly a hundred cache references, a datacenter round trip roughly five thousand memory references, a disk seek roughly twenty datacenter round trips.

The conclusion I would state explicitly, because it inverts most instincts: writes to the network within a datacenter are much faster than writes to local disk. The arithmetic is simple by design. Bandwidth is rate times size. Storage is count times size times replication, since what you buy is not what you store. Concurrency is arrival rate times duration, and the trap is that duration means time in the system including waiting rather than service time.

The caution is about the constants: they age at different rates, bandwidth improving far faster than latency, so an estimate can go wrong without the design changing, and invisibly. Ratios drift more slowly than absolutes, which is why I would memorise relationships and re-derive numbers.

And the discipline that makes an estimate useful to anyone else is writing the assumptions beside the answer, so it can be rechecked rather than believed or dismissed.
